title: How do you pronounce lieutenant? | MILITARY WORDS

entries.note: From Germanic-influenced Norman French rather than Parisian French, whose word is [[see:guerre]]; its Proto-Indo-European root meant to confuse or mix up.
The modern French word for war, showing the G where Norman French had the W that gave English [[same-root:war]].
Taken from Norman French with a W, while the Parisian form of the same word gave [[same-root:guardian]].
The Parisian French counterpart of Norman French [[same-root:warden]], showing the W/G split.
Another Norman French W word, paired with the Parisian-derived [[same-root:guarantee]].
The Parisian French counterpart of [[same-root:warranty]].
Rob thinks the US state is named after someone surnamed De La Warr, Norman for 'of the war'; Jess says it's the state she most often forgets exists.
The Latin word for war, literally struggle or strife; some languages may avoid it because it resembles [[see:bella]], and it survives in English derivatives.
Romance word for beauty that Latin [[see:bellum]] too closely resembles.
The justification for war, from [[from:bellum]]; the hosts joke that it sounds like the justification for your beauty.
Describes someone prone to conflict; from Latin [[from:bellum]].
Describes someone prone to conflict; from Latin [[from:bellum]].
Literally 'before the war', from [[from:bellum]]; often refers to the American South before the Civil War.
Another English word built on Latin [[from:bellum]].
From a root meaning to beat or fight, like [[same-root:combat]]; the -le ending is frequentative, so it means beating repeatedly.
Shares a root meaning to beat or fight with [[same-root:battle]]; literally fighting together.
The town where the Battle of Hastings was fought, now simply named after the [[see:battle]].
Means striking together, sharing a root meaning to strike with [[same-root:inflict]] and [[same-root:afflict]].
Shares the root meaning to strike with [[same-root:conflict]].
Shares the root meaning to strike with [[same-root:conflict]].
A Germanic personal name containing a word for war; it basically means fighting a battle.
A Germanic name whose element hild relates to battle, the name meaning literally armed for battle.
Thought to come from the woman's name [[from:Gunnhilda]] via [[see:Domina Gunilda]], a 1330 Windsor ballista; Middle English Gunilda for cannon was shortened to gonne.
Scandinavian woman's name formed of two elements meaning war or battle, from Old Norse [[from:gunnr]]; its shortening gave [[gave:gun]].
Name of a particularly large ballista in a 1330 Windsor Castle munitions inventory, an early link between [[see:Gunnhilda]] and [[see:gun]].
In Old English it was also a euphemism for a penis, which the hosts note surprises no one.
A top British rank, though marshal comes via French from a Frankish word for horse servant, so Rob ranks it lowest.
A variant of the same word as [[same-root:servant]], so Rob ranks it above the horse-servant [[see:field marshal]].
The same word as [[same-root:sergeant]] in a different form.
Originally meant a servant or boy, as its German cognate [[same-root:Knecht]] still does; German uses [[equivalent:Ritter]] for a knight.
German cognate of [[same-root:knight]] that still means a kind of servant.
The German word for a [[equivalent:knight]], familiar from the chocolate brand [[see:Ritter Sport]].
Chocolate brand cited to illustrate [[see:Ritter]]; the hosts mostly see it in airports.
Said to be the most common Old English word for a young boy, reflecting the early sense of [[see:knight]].
A slightly confusing rank in Rob's reranking, because [[see:major]] simply means big.
Rank whose fairly obvious etymology means big.
A rank that just means head, one of the many English derivatives of Latin [[from:caput]].
Latin for head, a recurring topic for the hosts because of its many English derivatives, including [[gave:captain]], [[gave:chapter]], [[gave:capital]] and [[gave:decapitate]].
One of the obvious English derivatives of Latin [[from:caput]], head.
One of the obvious English derivatives of Latin [[from:caput]], head.
One of the obvious English derivatives of Latin [[from:caput]], head.
Seems to mean body, as in [[see:corporal punishment]], but is disputedly thought to come via French [[from?:caporal]] from Latin for head.
Punishment of the body, cited to show why the rank [[see:corporal]] seems to mean body.
From French [[from:lieu tenant]], placeholder; the British 'left tenant' may come from U/V confusion or a French breathy ending, not from standing to the left.
Its split US/UK pronunciation is compared with [[see:lieutenant]], reversed.
A general officer is generally in charge; titles like [[see:lieutenant general]] and [[see:major general]] put the adjective after the noun, French-style.
Title in which 'general' is the adjective placed after the noun, showing French influence on [[see:general]].
Title in which 'general' is the adjective placed after the noun, showing French influence on [[see:general]].
Possibly because fighters were hired for a private cause in private armies, which is also why [[same-root:privateer]]s are so called.
Guns for hire, named for the same private-cause idea as [[same-root:private]].
From Latin [[from:solidus]], a gold coin: a soldier is someone paid to fight.
Originally a soldier's pension for buying salt.
Related to [[same-root:market]] and [[same-root:commerce]]; from the 14th to 17th centuries it meant anyone working for hire, now mainly soldiers; possibly linked to [[same-root?:Mercury]].
Related to [[same-root:mercenary]].
Related to [[same-root:mercenary]].
Related to [[same-root:mercenary]], from a root meaning wares.
Related to [[same-root:mercenary]], from a root meaning wares.
God of messengers, travellers and merchants, possibly related to [[same-root?:mercenary]]; his name is thought to be borrowed from an Etruscan god of exchange.
The least expected relative of [[same-root:mercenary]], implying heavenly rewards earned by God's devoted servants.
Related to [[same-root:infant]]: the young, inexperienced troops sent onto the battlefield first.
Literally 'not speaking', since infants cannot speak; related to [[same-root:infantry]].
From Latin [[from:caballus]], workhorse or packhorse, for mounted troops; [[same-root:chivalry]] has the same root.
From the same horse root as [[same-root:cavalry]].
Pronounced 'kernel' from French [[from:coronel]], but spelled after Italian [[from:colonnello]] during a vogue for Italian warfare; the head of a column of soldiers.
From an Italian cry, 'to arms', one of several terms from Italian warfare.
From Italian [[from:all'erta]], a call to go to the watchtower; the 'al' is the preposition 'to', not 'all'.
A Roman military term meaning commander of a hundred.
A Roman body of troops, which Rob thinks numbered about 5,000 to 6,000; gave [[gave:legionnaire]].
A soldier of a [[from:legion]], one of many.
Etymologically to reduce by a tenth, after a rare Roman punishment, but long used for utter destruction; pedants are wrong to insist otherwise.
Previously discussed; it no longer has to involve a fable, showing why etymology can't dictate meaning, as with [[see:decimate]].
From [[from:sluagh-ghairm]], a Scottish Highlanders' Gaelic war cry; other English renderings included [[see:slughorn]].
Highlanders' war cry, from sluagh, a demon or horde, and gairm, shout; gave [[gave:slogan]], and its second element relates to [[same-root:garrulous]].
An alternative English rendering of the Gaelic war cry that lost out to [[see:slogan]]; Jess thinks it would be a good marketing company name.
Means talkative; it came to English via Latin but shares a root with the second element of the Gaelic source of [[same-root:slogan]].
Originally [[from:gantlope]], a corridor punishment; it was conflated with [[see:throw down the gauntlet]], a mix-up like [[see:we'll burn that bridge when we come to it]].
Perhaps from Swedish, with a 'lope' like German [[same-root:laufen]]; a military punishment in which the culprit ran between two rows of men striking him.
To challenge someone to a duel by throwing your glove on the floor; conflated with [[see:run the gauntlet]].

entries.term: we'll burn that bridge when we come to it
entries.note: A blended saying the hosts compare with the mix-up behind [[see:run the gauntlet]].
From a French term for a small glove, related to modern French [[from:gant]], glove.
German word, meaning to walk, related to the 'lope' of [[same-root:gantlope]].
Shin or leg armour, from an Old French word for shin; like most armour, named after the body part it covers.
Shoulder armour, also called [[same-root:spaulders]], from a French word meaning shoulder.
Another name for [[same-root:pauldrons]], shoulder armour, from a French word for shoulder.
Forearm armour, from French avant-bras, forearm.
Throat armour, from the word for throat also seen in [[same-root:gorgeous]].
Originally described someone with a long, slender, shapely neck; shares the throat word in [[same-root:gorget]].
A neck protector, from Old Frankish.
Foot armour, from French sabot, shoe or clog, as in [[same-root:sabotage]].
Previously discussed as implying throwing shoes into the machine; from sabot, clog, like [[same-root:sabatons]].
Possibly from a military trial where the accused soldier faced the drum squad as charges were read out; one theory, but a good one.
US military acronym for 'f***ed up beyond all recognition' (or reason), admired for its withering scepticism, like [[see:SNAFU]].
US military acronym for 'situation normal, all f***ed up', which gave its name to the cartoon [[see:Private Snafu]].
WWII US military training cartoon, possibly voiced by [[see:Mel Blanc]], about a lowest-common-denominator soldier showing how not to behave; named after [[from:SNAFU]].
American military slang for rushing troops into position only to have them stand around for hours.
A military term now used beyond the military, with a fairly obvious origin.
A military term now used beyond the military, with a fairly obvious origin.
Now a low-level labourer; in the Vietnam War, an infantryman, from the grunting of exertion rather than pigs.
Literally sitting, as besiegers camp outside walls until the defenders give in; French siège means seat.
Very literal: to hide in a bush and jump out at someone.
Means made of barrels, a blockade originally of barrels, rocks and dirt; an old Latin word for one was [[see:cumulus]].
Old Latin word for a [[see:barricade]], meaning a mound, like cumulus clouds; related to [[same-root:encumbrance]].
Related to [[same-root:cumulus]], a blockage.
In English from the 1580s; ultimately from an onomatopoeic Greek word for boom; first meant mortar shells, famously used at the [[see:siege of Constantinople]].
Means to clap outward, related to [[same-root:applaud]], which Jess finds more accurate than boom; [[see:implode]] is much more recent.
Related to [[same-root:explode]], to clap outward.
To clap inward; much more recent than [[see:explode]], probably existing only because explosion existed.
The 1453 siege, thought to be the earliest and most famous use of mortars, the first things called [[see:bomb]]s.
A British WWI code name, passing the vehicles off as water tanks; the Caterpillar Machine Gun Destroyer was also codenamed [[see:cistern]] and [[see:reservoir]].
An alternative code name for the [[see:tank]] that didn't stick.
An alternative code name for the [[see:tank]] that didn't stick.
From Latin [[from:canna]], reed or tube, and related to [[same-root:cane]].
Confirmed on the spot as related to [[same-root:cannon]].
Named after [[see:Bob Burns]]'s comically large junkyard trombone from 1930s comedy, itself from [[from:bazoo]]; a big mouthy gun.
An older word from the 1800s for mouth or boastful talk, the basis of [[gave:bazooka]].
Latin for the electric ray, from a word meaning to be numb, like [[same-root:torpor]]; used from 1776 for a floating mine, later self-propelled explosives.
Related to [[same-root:torpedo]] through the sense of numbness.
Related to [[same-root:pomegranate]], from Latin granatum, seeded; early grenades looked like pomegranates.
Literally a seedy apple, from Latin granatum, seeded; related to [[same-root:grenade]].
Quite literally something curved.
Quite literally a stabber, something you dag someone with, prompting Jess's joke about [[see:dagnabbit]].
Jess jokes that the dag of [[see:dagger]] makes sense of it; Rob thinks she got lucky.
Means something that cuts or hurts, and was sometimes a euphemism for a penis, whose sheath is a [[see:vagina]].
Literally the sheath you put a [[see:sword]] in.
Coined at Confederate [[see:Andersonville Prison]] for a perimeter line that prisoners would be shot dead for crossing; now any boundary, like homework deadlines.
Confederate prison in the American Civil War where the [[see:deadline]] was drawn.
From [[from:casual]] in the old sense of happening by chance: people killed or injured incidentally; also the British name for the emergency room.
Meant happening by chance until the 'informal' sense arose in the late 19th century; gave [[gave:casualty]].
The more common current British name for the hospital department long called [[see:casualty]].
Popular British Saturday-night TV drama, basically a British ER, set in an accident and emergency department, named after [[from:casualty]].
Seems to mean a final shot on your way out, but it was originally a [[from:Parthian shot]], so its obvious explanation is folk etymology.
Parthian horsemen fired missiles backward while fleeing or pretending to flee; the phrase became [[gave:parting shot]].
